title: Moderate in all
hookLine: yoga is for one moderate in eating, sleep, work and play (Bhagavad Gita 6.17)
tomorrow: Arjuna objects: what if the mind just won't sit still?

lines: A SEAT: NOT TOO HIGH, NOT TOO LOW.
cards: Some instructions are oddly specific. A recipe that wants the eggs at room temperature. A coach who fixes your grip before you lift anything.
The Gita has one of those, and it's strange. Armies are waiting. Arjuna's whole world is at stake.
And in chapter six, Krishna stops to describe a seat: in a clean place, firm, not too high and not too low, with grass, a deerskin and a cloth laid over it. So, yesterday's question.
Why would a god on a battlefield care how high your seat is?

teach.h: THE SEAT IS THE LESSON IN SMALL.
teach.b: Because the seat is the whole lesson in small. Keep reading, and the same pattern spreads to the whole life.

teach.h: NOT TOO MUCH, NOT NONE AT ALL.
teach.b: Yoga, Krishna says, isn't for the one who eats too much, nor for the one who doesn't eat at all; not for the one who sleeps too much, nor for the one who keeps awake.
Then the verse that sums it up: for the one measured in food and recreation, measured in effort at work, measured in sleep and waking, yoga becomes the destroyer of sorrow.

The word in the verse for measured is yukta: fitted, balanced, just right, and it comes three times in one line. So, the puzzle solved. The Gita's yoga isn't won by the biggest fast or the longest night awake.
The seat isn't a throne, and it isn't the bare ground; neither is the life.

teach.h: EVEN PLAY IS ON THE LIST.
teach.b: Something worth repeating: in a book set on a battlefield, the yogi's list of balance includes recreation, right alongside work and sleep.
So the teaching is this: in the Gita, a steady mind rests on a body that is neither starved nor stuffed, neither sleepless nor sleeping the day away.
Moderate, so the mind can sit still.

how: In the Gita's sixth chapter, Krishna describes the meditator's seat and the measured life around it; people who practice from the Gita read these verses as plain guidance for sitting.

o: measured in food, sleep, work and play, never extreme
doing a little of everything, without any focus
giving up food and sleep to prove your devotion

games.q: the Gita's measure, piece by piece: tap the pairs.
p: not too high, not too low
not too much, not none at all
not too much, not kept awake

s: the Gita says real yoga means fasting and staying awake
6.16: yoga isn't for the one who eats nothing, or for the one who keeps awake.
the Gita's list of balance includes recreation
6.17 names food and recreation, effort in work, sleep and waking.
Krishna's seat should be raised high, like a throne
6.11: a firm seat in a clean place, not too high and not too low.

games.q: a friend starting meditation wants to sit for three hours on day one to do it properly. what does Gita 6 point to?
o: a measured sit that fits the rest of the day; yoga isn't extreme.
go for the three hours; the Gita praises whoever pushes hardest.
skip the sitting; the Gita cares about balance, not about practice.
games.why: in 6.16–17, yoga belongs to the one who is measured; even the seat is not too high and not too low.

practice: Sit on whatever is under you and find the middle: not slumped, not stiff. Let the head, neck and back line up, the way the Gita describes the seated yogi, and let the breath keep its own pace.
Whenever you lean too far either way, come back to center.

wordCard.voice: Moderate in all: the Gita's yukta, measured just right, in eating, sleep, work and play.

orig.note: Sanskrit, Bhagavad Gita 6.17: for one measured in food and recreation.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: moderate, not a fast and not a feast. Five of six from the Gita.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 6.10–13 (a clean place; a firm seat, not too high, not too low, of grass, deerskin and cloth; body, head and neck held erect and still)

Bhagavad Gita 6.16–17 (yoga is not for one who eats too much or not at all, sleeps too much or keeps awake; for one measured in food and recreation, in effort at work, in sleep and waking, yoga destroys sorrow)
